speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since the Prime Minister and about ten of his ministers are paying a one week's visit to British Columbia while the House is peacefully in session, and since British Columbia has been administered for several decades by Social Credit governments, which accounts for the fact that that province is ahead of many Canadian provinces as far as the prosperity of its people is concerned, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That this House immediately consider the opportunity of asking the Prime Minister as soon as he returns from his training session in administration and management by the Social Credit government of British Columbia to table in the House a complete report about all he has learned about efficient administration, so that all Liberal backbenchers who were unable to take the trip may profit from the British Columbia experience.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It appears that Security Advisory Services of the United Kingdom is the body recruiting mercenaries in England for service in Angola with funds provided by the CIA. This organization has caused an advertisement to be put in the Globe and
Mail of February 10, 1976, in effect seeking to enlist the services of Canadians as mercenaries, contrary to the provisions of the Foreign Enlistment Act, section 11, which prohibits any person from recruiting or otherwise inducing any person to enlist in armed services operating in another state.
Therefore, and in view of the resolution passed by this House opposing all armed intervention in Angola, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) be directed to investigate this matter forthwith and if the facts disclose an offence or offences against the Foreign Enlistment Act, to take the necessary proceedings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the evidence produced by a former safety inspector for Trans-Canada Pipelines and offered to the National Energy Board by the CTV television network to substantiate allegations that welding done on substantial sections of the Trans-Canada pipeline running through Manitoba and Ontario are of such poor quality as to constitute a safety hazard has yet to be examined by the National Energy Board, although it is freely available, and further that the chairman of the National Energy Board, Marshall Crowe, has issued a press release expressing his complete confidence in the safety of the line without having examined the evidence, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House directs the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) in his responsibility for the National Energy Board, to instruct the chairman of the Board itself to examine any evidence offered to them by the CTV television network to assure the safety of the Trans-Canada pipeline beyond any reasonable doubt, before any further reports are released by the Board for public consumption.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the CBC radio this morning carried a news story to the effect that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been reported as stating in Victoria yesterday that he would resign as Prime Minister if capital punishment were approved by the House of Commons, and in view of the fact that there are some abolitionists in all parties who have now been placed in the most difficult quandary of determining what this nation needs most, that is, capital punishment, abolition, or a new prime minister, I move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt):
That the Prime Minister be invited either to withdraw his statement or resign, preferably the latter.

speechtext: The "Pierced Vertical Form" which graces the grounds of the Official Residence of the Prime Minister is on loan from the National Gallery of Canada. It is the work of Dame Barbara Hepworth, D.B.E., whose contribution to twentieth-century sculpture was so significant as to achieve for her early international recognition. In the decades from her first exhibition in London in the year 1928, until her tragic death in a fire at her Cornish studio in St. Ives on May 21 of last year, she had exhibitions in numerous countries including of course the U.S.A. and Canada. Her works can be found in scores of collections and museums around the world. In Canada, the Vancouver Art Gallery and the National Gallery own some of her works. Among many distinctions accorded her are the Commission by the United Nations, in 1963, to make the abstract bronze in memory of Dag Hammarskjold to stand outside the United Nations Secretariat in New York City, and in 1970, the award of Le Grand Prix International de l'Art Feminin. The "Pierced Vertical Form", made of Nebrasina stone, is part of the acquisition program of the National Gallery of Canada aiming at gathering in Canada representative works of outstanding artists. Public funds for this acquisition program are subject to Parliamentary approval in the normal way through the approval of estimates. It is judged preferable not to disclose as a rule the acquisition cost of individual items as it might invite comparisons between artists or their agents or preclude the possibility that items might be acquired at a cost below their market value. The "Pierced Vertical Form" was acquired by the National Gallery of Canada in May 1966.

speechtext:
That the Seventh Report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, presented to the House on Tuesday, December 16, 1975, be concurred in, and that the committee be authorized to examine the matters referred to in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of the said report during the balance of this session.
He said: Mr. Speaker, some years ago when I first came to this place I was told one should always make one's speech as if it were one's last speech. Feeling the way I do today that might be more prophetic than otherwise. In any event I can claim to be about as representative of my area of Canada as anyone could be in this regard. My area is ravaged by approximately 30 per cent influenza and I think that after I have battled it for a week I probably have at least 30 per cent influenza. In any event, Sir, I will try to do the best I can on a subject which I regard as important and on which the House has given certain of us special responsibilities for more than a year. I hope we can persuade the House that the motion which stands before the House today amended somewhat should receive the favour of the House.
Perhaps my main job will be to outline more or less what we have attempted to do in respect of the task that was set before us, and how we have handled it in the last year or so. The task originally started in the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. In addition to the multitude of orders in council, regulations and other directives from government or government departments that could be considered to be statutory instruments, all of which amounted to at least 1,000 documents a year, it was also considered that this particular committee, which was a joint committee of both Houses, should look into two other matters. One concerned the guidelines the government uses in dealing with notices of motions for the production of papers. The second reference to the steering committee concerned the subject matter of a bill that has been dear to the heart of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the House leader for the Conservative party, for a good number of years.
I think it can be said, without paying exceptional favour to one member, that to consider the matter of freedom of information, which is what we are dealing with, without knowing the role of the hon. member for Peace River would be like staging Romeo and Juliet without at least one balcony. The hon. member for Peace River has over the years, going back at least a decade in my recollection, and surely for most of his parliamentary career, concerned himself with the subject of freedom of information. I hope he will be taking part in the debate later today, so I shall not dare to anticipate the wisdom he will give the House.
We had these two references to the committee: first, the guidelines which should govern us in dealing with notices of motions for the production of papers and, second, the subject matter of the freedom of information bill. How have we responded thereto? I think we have responded in

February 12, 1976
Statutory Instruments
a pretty reasonable way. We held 15 or 20 meetings to deal with those two topics. I should like to acquaint the House with the witnesses who appeared before the committee. We had the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp); we had Professor Donald C. Rowat of the academic community; we had Dr. Davidson Dunton who is now president of the Ontario Press Council. Dr. Dunton, as many of us will realize, was president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a noted academic as president of Carle-ton University and one very familiar with the intricate relations, if I may use that term, between government, government departments and the public.
We also had before the committee the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) in his then capacity as parliamentary secretary to the President of the Privy Council. We had before us Miss Lise Paquette, who had an official position in the Privy Council office, I believe, with regard to the answering of members' questions, and we had the hon. member for Peace River. We had such distinguished public servants as the former Clerk of the Privy Council, Gordon Robertson, Dr. Gordon Smith and Mr. D. F. Wall. We had some young civil libertarians from the Ottawa community. We had that well known intellectual public servant, private servant and university servant, Dr. Maxwell Cohen, and we had the awesome figure of Robert Cooper who is the ombudsman for CBC. Those were our witnesses in addition, I might say-and I will refer to this again in a few moments-to people of the committee itself.
We arranged a trip to the U.S.A., to Washington, where we studied the freedom of information act which came out originally in an early Kennedy year and then was amended in a Nixon year-quite a remarkable piece of legislation, more particularly as it was amended in the post-Watergate situation. We dealt there with members of the executive and members of the Senate and the House who were responsible in large measure for bringing this act about. We dealt there with what I would call the Nader group for short, but I would identify them as those who espoused particularly the interests of special or general consumer groups. We had the advantage of all those people in dealing with how a freedom of information act should operate. We heard from the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on their impressions of the operation of the acts dealing with freedom of information in Sweden, in Finland, in Russia and in other countries: we had the advantage of all their thinking. After hearing all this evidence, we have found ourselves probably with more questions to be answered than when we started out-very important questions as to whether a freedom of information set-up can properly be advanced in Canada.
I will not argue this afternoon for any particular school of thought with regard to freedom of information, but I might well venture one or two of my personal prejudices on this subject. What I am doing, on behalf of the members of the committee, Mr. Speaker and members of the House, is asking that the study be extended. I think we have to hear, for example, from people such as the dominion archivists about the release of information in its time.
I think we should have the parliamentary librarian, and other witnesses probably from the academic community.
I suspect that as a result of what we have heard from the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the United States we must have before us either the RCMP or at least representatives of police associations to deal with the matter of freedom of information. I hope I will be allowed to beg off these particular specialties as to police information, because I am confident that my parliamentary colleagues will rush to a rather fading voice and tell us something about what was heard in Washington when we talked to members of the Federal Bureau of Investigation to find out the problems they have encountered under the freedom of information act.
I should like to put a couple of quotations on the record. The first is an excerpt from a hearing which the committee held on Tuesday, February 25, 1975-almost a year ago-when we had before us Professor Donald C. Rowat who was then, and perhaps is now, president of the Canadian Political Science Association. He made the following point about going to Sweden to study the openness of the Swedish system with regard to the provision of information. At page 15:9 of our proceedings of that day he is recorded as having said the following. He is referring to a reporter of the Swedish equivalent of the Canadian Press, that is, the big, national press agency in Stockholm. He had discussions with them and they asked him to accompany one of the reporters who was going on his rounds to government departments the next day. That was arranged, and he went with the reporter. This is the eye-opener, and I hope that the following words will be remembered by everybody when they make up their minds tonight on this debate. Professor Rowat said:
So I went with him and, to my amazement, I found that in every government ministry and department there was a press room where the incoming and outgoing mail was laid out each morning for an hour. Now, this did interfere a little bit with government work as these documents and files were not available to the civil servants while they were laid out in the press room.
In other words, there was an opportunity for members of the press, at least on behalf of the public, to go into these government departments and find out what was in the mind of the citizens of Sweden. To me that was an eye-opener. Even the prime minister's office in that country could be held open to inspection as to what occupied people's minds. We simply do not have that sort of system here. Whether we want it here is another question. It may be that members would think that this is going a little too far, or they may think it goes very much too far-I do not know that-but I would think that, at first blush at least, it is a recognition that a more candid view of the operations of government should be available to the public.
The other quotation I would like to put on the record is from Dr. Davidson Dunton who gave evidence to the committee on Tuesday, March 4. There is a lot of material that should be read and studied by hon. members with regard to this important topic, but I will not attempt to read much more. I thought that Dr. Dunton put it as well as anybody when he said, as recorded at page 17:5 of that issue:
It is our view that in a situation like this, government should be much more open than it is. Citizens-not just people in the government-should have a right to the greatest possible amount of information about things the government is doing or will do and therefore will affect the lives of citizens and which, incidentally, citizens are paying for.

February 12, 1976

Over and over again we had, in the deliberations of the committee, in the correspondence that each of us received and, I dare say, in the correspondence that members of the public sent to us for our attention, the question as to why they cannot find out about this or that. They say that the government commissioned a study on, let us say, the safety of snowmobiles, and why should all that be stuck away behind some departmental privilege? Should it not be out in the open? When people are paid through our taxes to carry out studies which involve the health and well-being of the citizens of Canada, why cannot everyone know about it?
These complaints have come in. Mr. Cooper, the CBC ombudsman, gave us half a dozen. One of the reasons I hope the House will accept the motion today is that we are now getting answers from government departments, but because we referred the subject matter to the House, as we did just before Christmas, it is felt that these answers really cannot be studied or made public until we have our terms of reference back again. That may seem like a very technical point, but in this business where technicalities sometimes are very important we have to consider that sort of thing. I have tried to give my remarks some flavour; I realize not perfectly, but others will make up for my deficiencies with hearts, spades and more pizzazz that I am able to muster.
With regard to the future of the operations of the committee, there is at least one group which would like to come before us to make its presentation. The members of the Canadian Bar are starting to assemble some thoughts on the matter of freedom of information. From time to time overtures have been made to the parliamentary press gallery, the lone representation of which today is certainly a fighter for freedom of information. He is the man who took on the Nova Scotia censor board singlehandedly and has done rather well for himself. In any event, we hope the parliamentary press gallery will concern itself with a topic which must bother its representatives in their day-to-day activities in Ottawa.
I said I would not give very many thoughts of my own on this topic, and I will not, except that I hope two things will happen. First, I hope that the whole matter can be turned around and the basis will be that there should be such a policy of openness that departments, bureaucrats, ministers and the like who want to keep something back would have to establish why information should be withheld. That is just a personal feeling. The second thing is that from the moment of inception of a freedom of information act it would be regarded as essential by all ministries that from the moment a file is opened the material in that file should see the light of public scrutiny at the request of any reasonable person who comes, without any special animus, to see it.
While I have not presented the matter with any great nerve-and I cannot-I hope that with those two thoughts in mind the House will give consideration to the motion which stands in the name of myself, seconded by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore, and that we will be given back the mandate to carry on the studies. I think the House would indeed be pleased with what we come up with in, say, several months' time.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGULATIONS AND OTHER STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS-CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the chairman of the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, and also his co-chairman, Senator Forsey from the other place, for the job they have done in leading the committee and trying to keep the committee on the rails in spite of its particular desire to go off and follow its own hobby horses. It would be remiss of me, also, if I did not congratulate the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) who should be feeling quite happy today-a man who has fought to have this subject aired before the House of Commons. He has had some notable accomplishments and has seen some progress being made with regard to resolving the problems which he has been prominent in bringing to the attention of the House.
I believe this is an important debate because to some extent it will dictate the kind of government we will have in the future. The kinds of solutions to the problems the government faces are largely wrapped up in the amount of information which is made available to citizens in the complex world in which we live.
I come to the matter of dealing with freedom of information, not out of any ideological bent but from a practical point of view after having served for 2'A years as parliamentary secretary to presidents of the privy council. One of the things which has sparked my attention has been the fact that the person or the group which is hurt most by the secrecy of government is the government itself. One of the difficulties we have is that in a complex society there is a tendency for governments and others to think that they, indeed, have all the information required to make a particular set of decisions. In point of fact, when one looks at those decisions and when one looks at the supporting information behind those decisions, it becomes perfectly clear that the greatest victims of secrecy are governments themselves.
I do not think it is necessary to give many examples: two will be sufficient. The first example is that since we have entered into the anti-inflation program nowhere have I seen, in any of the documents the government has provided, a reasonable, full and complete explanation of why the government changed its mind at the time it did and went into the program. In view of the fact that there are some sectors of our society opposed to the program, it seems this is a rather unfortunate omission, particularly since most of the statistical information and other arguments are readily available. Here is an example of how the government has managed to hurt itself.
Let me give another example of the limitations the government automatically imposes upon itself by not making available to citizens the data bases on which it bases its decisions. When we went into the anti-inflation program, the government in its wisdom considered that there were approximately 1,500 firms in Canada which fitted under the guidelines, that is, those which had more than 500 employees. Now that we are into the program, what do we find? We find that the number now is approximately 6,500, and still rising. Out of a desire to protect itself and its own deliberations, the government has made decisions and has hurt itself in trying to convince Canadians of the adequacy of the course it is following, and it has

February 12, 1976
Statutory Instruments
made decisions which seem to be incorrect on the basis of the information that was its own data basis.
It seems to me that in the complex society in which we live, where the issues are very difficult to comprehend, even for the experts-and there are too many experts-we very often do not have an opportunity to have their discussions and preliminary decisions aired to a wider range of people so that the holes therein can be picked at, discovered and corrected; and the people who suffer most are the Canadian people who elect a government which has a fear of providing this additional information. So I want to say at the onset that I fully support the motion. I hope the House will support it, and I hope the government will take to heart the findings and discoveries which are slowly coming to it, one of them being that the government itself and the party in power often is hurt more by this excessive devotion to secrecy than anyone else.
It seems to me that the function of debate in the country and in the House is to explore in a reasonable way the alternatives available to the country, and for the House and the government to decide just what is best for us all. Nobody wins in the game of politics when we make wrong decisions based on inadequate information, which so often is the case and as we have before us in the current set of circumstances. I want to emphasize my support and the fact that I believe we are on the verge of making some significant progress in this regard. I think credit should be given to the joint committee which has laboured on this matter and provided a focal point for Canadians interested in the subject.
I have noted the dilemma the government faces in terms of the inadequate data base and the assumptions it makes that it has an adequate one. It is difficult to have debate in this country if we do not have some information on the data base. One of the most frustrating things is to see debate in the House of Commons or in the country where participants are using separate bases of fact. In such cases, there can be no meeting of minds. In most cases, however, one can have fruitful debate where there is agreement on the basic facts. It strikes me that the government is the institution most capable of synthesizing the facts. Through a wide variety of sources it has a greater opportunity to make available the information in the bowels of its operations than it now does.
It is extraordinarily difficult to get the information out, and there are two reasons for that. The first is the desire of people within the civil service to protect their position, and the second is to some extent the socialization that goes on. When a person enters the civil service he feels that he must protect his data base and hold it for his superiors and the government. That means that when the ordinary citizen asks for information he is often met with a refusal, mainly because of this socialization. People prefer to protect themselves by not giving out information. It is built into the system, and that built-in bias is one of the things that must be dealt with. I do not deny that it will be difficult.
The second element often is the particular desire of departments or sections within departments to protect information they have obtained. The saying "knowledge is power" applies here. Very often it is difficult for the other
(Mr. Reid.]
sections of government to get that information or research. In my experience of trying to ferret out information for members of parliament I have found this one of the most difficult obstacles to overcome. It is also a psychological problem, and it has to be beaten.
I believe the first thing the committee should do is recommend that the existing guidelines for the production of papers-which is a matter before the committee now as a separate reference-be brought down in the form of legislation. I believe that psychologically that would give a great deal of impetus to breaking down the internal barriers that exist not only within the civil service but also among ministers. I think the very fact of putting those guidelines into legislation and amending them where required, so that the committee could come back with the recommendations and also the precise wording the government might use, would be helpful: it would be a constructive step. We would accomplish the end of putting the guidelines into statute law. If we were to include as a preamble the first sentence of the guidelines to the effect that the basic premise was to be that all information should be freely available, with the exceptions, the premise would override a great deal of the objections hon. members might have.
If we were to make that recommendation, we would also provide a speedy way of resolving the inevitable differences that occur, that is, that the government can choose who can have information and whether it should or should not be released. The system I would recommend, ideally, would be that used in Sweden. The hon. member for Peace River and I were quite surprised to find out that when there was conflict between members of the public for information and the bureaucracy which did not wish to provide it, those cases were settled within one day. If the matter went to the supreme administrative tribunal, it could take two or three days. The settlement of cases under freedom of information was considered a priority issue and was done swiftly, not by the courts but by the administrative tribunal. Perhaps one might want to think of a system that could be incorporated in a bill that would provide speedy resolution of these problems in a manner fair and consistent with our conditions.
My suggestion is to adapt the system used in the Unemployment Insurance Act. Where there is a dispute after the board of referees has made a decision on an appeal, one can appeal to the umpire. The umpire is a federal court judge acting as the final court of appeal under the system set up under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I believe that if one were to put in a proper time limit-say one working week-perhaps the federal court judge might not be available for this, but some other court could be developed and that would provide a speedy resolution to the problem of what was and what was not acceptable. It seems to me the jurisprudence would be relatively simple and there would be a quick way of solving the problem. At the present time, cabinet is the final court of appeal as to whether documents or information requested shall be released. This is, clearly, not satisfactory to all members of the House of Commons. In my experience, it was not always satisfactory to me as the person having some responsibility for the administration of the guidelines. I believe these would be a valuable series of recommendations. I believe the committee should take them and deal
February 12, 1976

with them as its first item of business once the current round of hearings has been completed.
The other problem that comes to mind is quite important, and that is the conflict between privacy and freedom of information. The example given by the chairman, of the Swedish system, whereby incoming mail to the government is exposed to the eyes of the world, and also the replies, strikes me as being a very unique set of circumstances and not one that I should care to see duplicated in Canada. I believe any citizen has the right to write to his member of parliament, his government, and to be sure that information is confidential between him and his government, between him and his member of parliament or, indeed, anybody else. I do not believe that I, as a third person, have the right to look upon anybody's correspondence with the government; that is correspondence that is private between the individual and the government.
I think for any kind of freedom of information we should be looking upon it from the point of view of whether there is conflict between freedom of information and the right to privacy. We should put emphasis on the right of privacy of individuals or organizations communicating with the government. That is fundamental to our kind of society, and I would hate to see it destroyed. This means that what we are doing, unlike the Swedish example, is ensuring that if I write to the Unemployment Insurance Commission or the Canada Pension Plan, my correspondence is private to those government organizations; it is not exposed to the press or to my neighbours. My relationship with my government should be on the same basis as my relationship with anybody else. They are private relations with the government; they are not open to the press and to neighbours.
Mr. Speaker, the other point I want to raise in conjunction with the privacy area is the related dilemma of organizations and individuals who have given information to the government, upon request, on the basis of its confidentiality, or even cases where the government has established programs where people are allowed to go in and participate and the information given to complete the application is also confidential. I believe that kind of confidentiality should continue to be engrained in our system. At the same time, I recognize there are going to be severe difficulties. It seems to me this will be a different question for the committee to work its way through.
There are also some related issues: the right of the government to discuss its policies and alternatives in privacy; the right of civil servants to make recommendations to their superiors and to the cabinet; the right for the internal dialogue in government to continue unabated; and the right of the government itself to reach its own conclusions in its own due course.
I distinguish between the concept of material and information that is factual and material and information based on opinion and conclusion. There must be such distinctions. The former minister of finance, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) said that only about 10 per cent of what is in a cabinet document really has to be secret. The only difficulty is that nobody agrees on which 10 per cent should be secret and which 90 per cent should

Statutory Instruments
be released to become public knowledge. If hon. members look at cabinet documents which have been published basically in the form of green papers, or at other cabinet documents which have been leaked from time to time, they will readily see that even cabinet documents, because of their structure, can give rise to different claims, different conclusions and even different recommendations. Without doubt, many other government documents structured in the same way should be dealt with in the same way. I submit that the result would be more information being made available to the Canadian people.
In the short time available to me I shall suggest a number of matters to the House and the committee which we must deal with as we consider these difficulties. First, there is the cost of the operation. Clearly, if we are to make more open our process of government and release more information, it will be more costly. An information network will need to be created; it will need to span the country; it will have to provide information quickly, and not delay it. Second, the issue of bilingualism arises. With the development of a bilingual capacity in the civil service, and as more and more high level civil servants can read and understand both languages, an inquiry can be brought to the attention of a civil servant in the language of the originator. The question then is, are the documents requested to go out in both languages or only one? Since we are discussing the principle of freedom of information, should not a document provided be in the language of the originator?
Third, we should look at time limits within which documents and material should be provided. Although I do not have any positive information, it strikes me that the ten working days provided in the American legislation is too short in view of the complexity of material being requested. That has been the complaint with regard to the American legislation. Perhaps we should consider a series of graduated times depending on the complexity of the information requested, or we might set a limit of 20 days. The committee should consider this. Fourth, we must remember, as we become more open, that there will be changes in the operation of the bureaucracy. We should consider this seriously and learn if this process will make the bureaucracy more efficient or less efficient, what the cost benefits will be and what the ultimate effects on the bureaucracy itself will be. I have mentioned the psychological impact which I think will take place even if we accept existing guidelines in legislative form. In my opinion, that should be counted as a considerable plus.
Fifth, we must consider the possible abuses which could arise under the legislation. It was clear, from the experience the hon. member for Peace River and I had in the Scandinavian countries, and clear from the experience in the United States, that there is a potential for abuse under the legislation, particularly in connection with regulatory bodies- and regulatory functions. In that area there is tremendous potential for abuse. Sixth, I should like to see a more precise definition as to what information is to be released if indeed we go beyond the guidelines. Information I touched on previously, such as that dealing with privacy, personal records and references to individuals within documents, should be considered as well.

February 12, 1976
Statutory Instruments
I know my time has almost ended. Let me make one more suggestion. Now that the committee is reaching the end of its work and has come to the end of its hearing of witnesses, the time has come for the government to come before us and present its position in clear terms. This would be most helpful. I invite the government to come before the committee and put forward a position which can be put into legislative form. It is time to do this. We can develop such ideas together in partnership and produce thereby a much better piece of legislation and a much better system of practice than we now have.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGULATIONS AND OTHER STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS-CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by commenting on the last suggestion of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). Of course the government will have to be consulted. We must know what they want to do. I hope the committee will formulate its own recommendations. If the government approves, very well; but the committee should tell the government what it thinks should be done in this area: the government should not tell the committee, as my hon. friend suggested. I do not object to consulting the government. If they have plans, I am sure we shall be glad to learn from them about those plans.
The core of the report we are considering has to do with support in principle for freedom of information legislation, which I regard as highly important. The committee's very name deters any great interest in what it does; its very title, "Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments", is calculated to keep people disinterested in the discussion in the committee. The freedom of information aspect of the committee's work affects every citizen, the operation of parliament and government generally. We should seek to destroy secrecy in government and its agencies. There is too much secrecy. Therefore, I personally approve the motion before the House. At least we can debate the principle or the idea that legislation dealing with this subject is necessary.
Without doubt, the events summed up in the word "Watergate" interest and concern the people and legislators of the United States. But Watergate does not affect them only. There is a widespread need for fuller information. We need to have an open, instead of a closed, society. Ralph Nader put it well when said:
A well informed citizenry is the lifeblood of democracy ...
In our policy, where the ultimate power is said to rest with the people, a free and prompt flow of information from government to people is essential to achieve the reality of citizen access to a more just governmental process.
What Ralph Nader said applies to Canada and other countries. We must consider two aspects of this matter: the right of parliament and members of parliament to secure information through the giving of notice and asking for disclosure of documents, and the right of the general public to secure information. Both aspects are highly important. Almost every member of parliament can think of matters on which he or she wished to obtain information but with respect to which the government, or an agency of government, refused to disclose information. This has happened to me in matters in which I take special interest, and no doubt almost every other member has had experience similar to mine when trying to secure information concerning various spheres of government.

I am thinking, for example, of external affairs. We have an agency known as CIDA, and this agency spends- rightly, in my judgment-a very substantial sum of money. I believe it is essential to the proper operation of CIDA that it should provide public access to information concerning its affairs. Yet a situation developed last session in which a document was prepared, at public expense, by chartered accountants dealing with the subject of the turnover of personnel employed by CIDA. Information contained in this document was refused us, initially by the president of CIDA but later by the then secretary of state for external affairs, now President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp). The matter was since raised once in the House and I know that the government used its majority to prevent disclosure of the document in question.
I think of another item which is very recent. We were told by the newspapers in the last day or two that a conference has taken place in London between representatives of seven countries able to produce nuclear reactors and nuclear materials. The conference related to safeguards and agreements as to safeguards so that those materials, when sold, could not be converted into nuclear weapons or, at least, that there was a better prospective of their not being so converted. This conference, Mr. Speaker, was supposed to be secret; no one was supposed to know about it. Here we find the people of the world, whose survival may depend upon effective safeguards, being told, "These matters are being discussed, but you cannot be told anything about what is taking place." I agree there are scientific details which perhaps ought not to be disclosed, but the substance of the discussions is something with which the world as a whole is concerned. Yet, as I say, the public in all countries was denied access to this information.
Again, most people who are interested in the environment know of reports on this subject which have been kept secret, perhaps because they do not suit the particular views of certain elements in bureaucracy, or else disclosed only under great pressure. The fact that they have been made, very often at great public expense, has little bearing on the attitude taken toward publication. In the field of immigration, for example, I know that material of great importance to the immigrant affecting the right to a hearing, review proceedings, and so on, are kept secret, sometimes in the form of guidelines which are never disclosed-not even in the Canada Gazette where one can sometimes find these things if one knows enough and looks long enough. Some of these documents which are relevant to the rights people have to a proper hearing are not disclosed, and the Department of Immigration says it has no intention of disclosing them. Indeed, in the special committee only after considerable effort were we able to obtain these documents. Many members of parliament could give similar illustrations of material which could be disclosed without the state being endangered in any way or without harm resulting to anybody. It is time this sort of secrecy became a thing of the past.
I commend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) upon his bill-it is a pioneer measure in this field- and for the fight he is putting up on this subject. He will probably agree with me that the bill he put forward is
February 12, 1976

capable of improvement. Nevertheless, the fact that he has brought it forward is an important link in the chain by which we are seeking, through the committee and through the work of parliament, to open the door a little upon what goes on in government. I believe this constitutes a great service to Canadians.
Of course there must be exceptions: nobody doubts this. There are matters of secrecy and there are certain types of confidentiality which require exceptions to be made. We should be careful, though, to ensure that those exceptions are carefully scrutinized to see that they are not a cover for the refusal of information which could perfectly well be disclosed. The framework should not be so loosely drawn as to enable anybody who felt so inclined to say that a particular document or piece of information fell within one category or another of exempted material and thus could be withheld.
I went, with other members, to Washington where we spent an extremely useful day discussing with officials there the United States freedom of information act. This is one field where they are ahead of us, Mr. Speaker. We do not like to think that in a political matter the United States is ahead of us, but in this particular area they are well ahead of us. They have had a form of information act for some time, but they found it to be defective and replaced it with a new one.
We spoke with people responsible for enforcing the act, and we spoke with people on the other side of the fence seeking to obtain information. We found that all parties agreed, in general terms, on the value and importance of the act and their appreciation of an open, as opposed to a secret, society. The 1974 amendments conferred upon every person the right to apply for information. Another thing they did was to provide for tribunals, with a right of appeal, of course, capable of enforcing disclosure and judging whether a claim for exemption was sound or not. This is absolutely essential.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is not in the House at the moment, but he mentioned that under our system-and this was confirmed by the President of the Privy Council when he gave evidence in the committee- when there is a dispute as to whether something should be disclosed or not, the issue is always decided by the government. Members of the House who are learned in the law know there is an ancient Latin maxim which says that no one should be a judge of his own case. Until there is a tribunal to enforce a decision, to interpret and apply it, we are left with paper which is really not worth too much. There must be provision for judicial or quasi-judicial review.
There are bound, of course, to be difficulties in working out the act, but those difficulties are in no way insuperable. I am sure there might be some nuisance applications for information, but I suppose procedures could be developed to deal with them. We should look to providing applicants with what they have in the United States through the activity of a sort of public interest agency, as they call it there. It is headed by Ralph Nader. I have in mind a body which would assist citizens who are seeking information and would advise them about the legal steps which may be necessary, including the filling in of required forms. I think that is absolutely essential.
Statutory Instruments
Then we must study any proposed freedom of information act in relation to rights to privacy. I would take issue, to a certain extent, with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I do not think it is a case of "either/or". I think on some matters the right to privacy should prevail; on other matters freedom of information on matters of public interest should prevail. I should not like to be categoric and say that the right to privacy always takes priority over the rights of the public.
As I said some time ago, the President of the Privy Council produced a series of guidelines which were supposed to be binding on parliament regarding production of papers, and suggest that we should legislate to make them effective. I think they are so defective that it would be better if we started at the beginning rather than copied them. There are all sorts of very vague exceptions. There is no adequate enforcement procedure. Indeed, the President of the Privy Council said that the decision whether something should actually be produced should always be left with the government. Be that as it may, I guess it was a step forward when these guidelines were produced.
There has been ample British precedent on this matter. We are supposed to have inherited our tendency toward secrecy in government from the British, but they have moved forward. The Franks commission, which made a report in 1972 on the Official Secrets Act, suggested there was a necessity to repeal the Official Secrets Act and replace it with another act that was far more limited in the exceptions it made in regard to publication of material. Here, again, I think we find a useful precedent. As has been mentioned, Sweden has had long experience in this regard. If we are inclined to think that it is a sort of easy option to make information available, that it will somehow damage the state or the security of the state, then I would remind hon. members that Sweden is a nation outstanding in many respects for its good government, lawfulness and the way in which it manages its own affairs.
I join with my colleagues in hoping that this motion will be passed and that it will give the committee the green light to proceed by taking the general principle that is already approved and putting it into some sort of detailed proposals or legislative form, as the case may be, so that a blow can be struck for freedom and for real democracy in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for the words they have spoken in connection with any slight participation I have had in this matter. Once again I would extend my thanks to the members of the committee for the objective and useful way in which the subject matter has been dealt with. When one looks back at the history of this particular project and other projects, one realizes that what we do today is simply the result of things that have been done before. While walking this morning through the corridors of this building, I met Mr. Barry Mather, formerly a distinguished member of the New Democratic Party in this House. Both Mr. Mather and I had bills along this same line of subject matter, at the same time, for two sessions. What has happened? We carried forward this idea for a while and today the idea has been merged into

the report of the committee. I hope that when this day is over the proposal will be merged into a report from the committee to the House on which the House will have pronounced itself. The torch will then go to the government in due course and the government will have some decisions to make.
There is a broader attitude to take toward this issue. For the last month or so, we in this House have been debating issues dealing with economics, inflation, employment and unemployment, law and order, stability, and social benefits for the people of this country. From what I have read of history, parliament in this country and parliaments in other parts of the world were debating issues like those 100 and 200 years ago. If I do not miss my guess, parliaments which succeed us-if parliaments still exist, as I hope they will-will be debating the same issues 200 years from this date.
It is very important to remember that these subject matters are not going to vanish. We are not going to pass laws to make all things good for all people. However, it is very important to make certain that the mechanisms and means that we adopt in this parliament for dealing with these problems are improved. This is something that lies squarely within our competence. There are some problems that we cannot solve, but we can solve the question of our ability as members and our capacity as a House to deal more effectively with these issues. I submit that to do so we have to bring into the decision on these issues the people of the country. We represent the people of Canada in a democracy, but in actual fact people in general participate only to a very slight extent in the decisions that are made. I think this is not because governments and civil servants are vicious or corrupt or bad; it is because they are remote and removed from the impact of the decisions that are made and from policies and spending programs.
When we pass an act that provides that parliament acts by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons, it is not really the case. Formally it is, but in actual practice it is not. I think the mechanisms and means by which we in parliament operate have to be altered and improved so that the people come into the picture as partners, even if only as junior partners, and feel that they are playing a real part in the decisions that are taken.
There is no doubt that in the few democracies that still exist in the world there is a growing gap between the governed and the governors. This is due to a number of factors. There has been cynicism, distrust, doubt, wonder and a feeling that the people are both helpless and hopeless. They have no means of knowing what the government is doing and why it is doing it. I think Watergate was a typical illustration of this. If you remember, Mr. Speaker, Watergate was only a fourth-rate burglary; but it was an attempt by people in authority to cover up problems that ultimately led to the downfall of a president of the United States. It is in that light that I think we should approach this matter as well as the more detailed issues that were raised by hon. members of the House who preceded me. I hope we will get the unanimous approval of members of all parties in the House, and that when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) speaks he will indicate that the government accepts the views set out in
the committee report calling for acceptance in principle of freedom of information legislation and for reference back to the committee of certain terms of reference that they have felt essential. In that sense, it may not then be necessary to call for a vote, as Mr. Speaker indicated was possible.
I say that because a unanimous decision of this House to support the view set out by the committee will have a very considerable effect on people in the civil service regarding the question of freedom of information. When they find they cannot beat us, maybe they will join us. Then, subject to the exceptions which I know must exist and to which the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and others have referred, there will in due course be put into place in this House, in this parliament and in this country, a method by which information will be made available. In 1972 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House that the-
-democratic process requires the ready availability of true and complete information. In this way people can objectively evaluate government policies. To act otherwise is to give way to despotic secrecy.
I should like to think the Prime Minister meant those words when he spoke them in 1972 at the time of the debate on and presentation of the task force on information. However, the conduct of the Prime Minister and the government since that time certainly has not given effect to what the Prime Minister said in 1972. I have the suspicion that he was persuaded by his advisers that there had to be a gap between what he said then and actual practice. His principal advisers were quite reluctant in respect of providing information, for a number of reasons, some of which were put forward quite persuasively by the civil servants who appeared before the committee. I think most people who ascend, collectively, the steps of government to the throne feel the same way. I suspect that if I were ever a member of the government-which does not seem very likely at my stage of political life-I would probably feel the same way.
It is essential for us to put into place in this House mechanisms and means by which it will not be possible from this time on for people in the bureaucracy and in the government to refuse to provide in a reasonable way the facts on which parliament must operate. The right to know and to be told the true facts is essential to government.
Today the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked about the details of certain agreements in respect of the sale of a CANDU project. He is entitled to that information on his own behalf, and on behalf of members of this House, just as the residents of the Port Hope area are entitled to be told the degree of radioactivity of the waste being poured into the lake and dumped in the vicinity of their homes. This matter is as important to the Leader of the Opposition, in his position, as it is to the people in the community of Port Hope. This principle is important to the members of this House who were inquiring a year ago about reports of bad meat being sold in the province of Quebec, and just as important to the native people living in the Yellowknife area who wanted to know the details of a report about arsenic poisoning in waters near the city of Yellowknife.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the motion before us which would continue and, indeed, expand the terms of reference of the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. This is an additional duty we are imposing on the committee, but I think members of the House generally would agree this is the most appropriate committee to deal with the matter of freedom of information.
It would be easy to take an extreme position on access to government information. The libertarian extreme would be to say that all government reports, papers and correspondence should be available to the people all the time without regard to context or circumstances. The closed-door extreme would be to insist that, because of the collective cabinet responsibility imposed by our system of responsible government, the only information which should be made known to the public would be statements formally released by the government. Most Canadians will find one extreme as unconvincing as the other.
If all government operations, without exception, were carried out in the public eye, the first casualty would be honest differences of opinion in the public service. Public servants would put in writing only what they thought the public was prepared to hear. In Sweden, for example, in every government department there is a press room where incoming and outgoing mail is laid out every morning for an hour for press and public inspection. Even such personal matters as income tax returns are open to public scrutiny. Consequently, what has happened is that paper has become much less important in government, and everything that really matters tends to be dealt with orally. Taken to the extreme, complete disclosure would seriously

impair the effectiveness of government. On the other hand, to limit public knowledge of government to what the government wanted the people to know would amount to a system of managed news and would be a step toward the horrors George Orwell saw for 1984.
Most Canadians would probably agree that the solution has to be a compromise, with a presumption in favour of disclosure, so that the people's right to information should receive maximum possible respect and attention. The thorny question is, what ought to be published? The exceptions allowed cannot be so extensive as to swallow up the rule of disclosure. Since the policy of making available as much information as possible must be balanced against such considerations as effective public administration, protection of the security of the state and rights of third parties to privacy, even the best-inten-tioned government finds it all too easy to resolve doubtful cases in the direction of secrecy.
The criteria to be applied might well be generally agreed. Security documents, personal correspondence, records and tax returns, legal opinions and matters relating to possible prosecutions should probably not be disclosed. Our system of responsible government also makes the disclosure of proceedings of cabinet meetings and draft government bills inappropriate. On the other hand, government green and white papers and royal commission reports should clearly be published, subject to the withholding of information on possible prosecutions. There should also be no question about the release of task force reports, studies by consultants or, generally, any government report or departmental document on a matter on which work has been completed. The grey area will probably lie in the determination of when work has been finished.
Given the natural inclination of any government to favour its own interest, and the fact that borderline areas do exist, what is needed is a device to strengthen the resolve of a well-intentioned government to disclose and to punish politically a government wishing to conceal. Canada needs an independent information authority which would be able to participate in the decision-making process-to decide what ought to be released and what ought to be withheld. Some suggest the judiciary as an outside authority with the public credibility to do the job. But the task, as I see it, is not of the odd-job variety-to scrutinize documents now and again. It would be an onerous daily task. In order to cope, I believe that the authority involved has to be close to the government process itself.
On the other hand, it would not do to confer the responsibility on an existing minister or department as, for example, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has been assigned the duty of reporting to parliament on federal laws which infringe upon the Canadian Bill of Rights. There is too much scope for conflict of interest to allow the government to be responsible for its own self-examination in so fundamental an area.
My proposal is for the establishment of an independent information advocate. This new office would be answerable to parliament rather than to the government itself. It would recommend what government information should
February 12, 1976

be made public and what should not. As an agency within government, the office of the information advocate could, if necessary, pry open every filing cabinet in the government service. In status and independence I would compare the information advocate with the Auditor General, who also exercises a supervisory authority, by parliamentary appointment, for the benefit of the public. In order to assure the advocate's public credibility, the government should propose to parliament, for appointment, a man or woman of unimpeachable independence and integrity. Perhaps he or she could be drawn from a panel recommended by the information media across the country. The advocate's tenure should be either indefinite or for a substantial length of time such as ten years. Within whatever term is adopted, tenure should be on the same basis as a judge's to ensure independence.
Because of the government's collective responsibility to govern, I would leave the ultimate decision whether to release information or not to the cabinet, but I would require the information advocate to report to parliament any instances in which his or her recommendations were not followed by the government. The government would then have to make a public defence. I believe that such a system would create a healthy tension between the cabinet and the advocate in which the government would be publicly challenged when it tried to withhold information which he or she deemed ought to be released. The information advocate, like the Auditor General, would be able to inform the public about things which might otherwise have been swept under the carpet and to require the government to reveal and defend its information practices when necessary.
It seems to me that such a system would preserve both the integrity of the government process-because the review would be from within-and the public's right to know what the government is doing so as to be able to judge it-because of the review itself. It would provide a necessary check on the government, but through a political rather than a legalistic remedy. Ultimately, the failure to disclose would itself be disclosed and that information would be put into the hands of the people for their decision.
It has been objected that, if the advocate made a report indicating reasons why a certain document ought to be disclosed, the content of the document would then be compromised. If reasons were not stated, I agree that public credibility would be lost. Obviously, at least general reasons would have to be advanced and the advocate's discretion as to the degree of disclosure trusted. We can do no better than to rely on the usual political processes and safeguards in such cases.
A freedom of information act enshrining the principle of public access to information would be a useful beginning, but in the absence of an independent authority to interpret it, it would not be a giant step forward. A belief that every government needs independently applied restraints is basic to democracy. As Francis Bacon wrote in a different context centuries ago, knowledge is power. The special committee on statutory instruments, which I had the honour to chair, put it this way in 1969:
There can be neither responsibility nor accountability when there is
no knowledge of what has been done. In political matters knowledge is
the beginning of power, and its lack, impotence.
Statutory Instruments
In a democracy, the people can have only as much power as they have knowledge; and an open government will want to ensure that as much power as possible remains with the people, because identification with the people provides a government with the best possible source of power. In conclusion, I might again say that I am pleased to support the motion which is before us today.

Mr. Speaker, this issue is one which will not go away. I feel somewhat as if I had been around the track several times, because it is the third debate in my time here on the matter of accessibility, accountability and openness in government. I recall very well the time when a person who is now on the treasury benches, the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), years ago took part in a debate. Of course, he was then supporting the concept of openness.
I think the issue was put very well, if I may paraphrase the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), when he said that it is time for the government to state its intention on the issue of public information. I think that is what the resolution proposes, that the committee will continue its deliberations and consider this question. But I had always hoped that Canada would be the bellwether country in the world. Perhaps other countries have long since made it difficult for us to catch up to them in the matter of openness, but I thought some years ago, when the Pearson government took a look at the whole matter of the Official Secrets Act, that there at least would be a rather forthright report. It turned out, rather sadly, that, through no fault of the then prime minister, it was a rather orthodox document, very much looking backward instead of forward, and very few changes were made in the Official Secrets Act. Now, as a result of the Franks Report in Great Britain and the commitments made by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, fundamental changes will be made to the Official Secrets Act in England. This, of course, was an opportunity that Canada once again missed. We could have led the western democracies. Instead of that we are stumbling along and still have not made a commitment.
I think it is right that we recall another important report that was made by a couple of excellent, dwas never allowed the free rein that the commission report recommended for it.
In the few minutes which I have, I propose to deal with the matter of ministerial responsibility and administrative secrecy and suggest several things dealing with government and the bureaucracy which have worshipped far too long at the altar of secrecy and anonymity. The attainment of greater freedom of information and openness in government will not come easily. We have seen that. It is 1976, and many of us are still worshipping at this altar. Several times over the past years I have spoken in the House about the need to, as Professor J. A. G. Griffith has stated-
-take the lid off the machinery of government, to see how it works, who says what to whom, at what level decisions are taken, what private criteria are used, how far politics is allowed to override those criteria, on what statistical and other facts the decisions are based: this wish does not derive only from curiosity or from party animosity but also from self-interest, from quis custodiet, and from a feeling that government represents another group interest.

February 12, 1976
Statutory Instruments
Perhaps I should identify the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) as being one of the few who might recognize that Latin phrase. I want his children and grandchildren, when they read this debate, to know that at least there was one. However, experience has demonstrated that there exists both in government and the bureaucracy tremendous resistance to scrutiny, openness and accountability. Such candour affronts ministerial and bureaucratic sensitivities. Douglas Fisher described this environment rather well when last December he wrote the following:
The bureaucrats will appeal-
As they have to the committee.
... to the principles of ministerial responsibility and their own anonymity. The politicians in power shiver over any eclipse of official secrecy. They fear the lot of the emperor without clothes.
We are confronted here with ministers clothed in secrecy, private dealings and anonymity. When I speak of private dealings, I do not mean the word "deal" in any pejorative or evil connotation. I mean that a deal has been made or an arrangement has been made, within the process, clothed with secrecy and probably if the arrangement was open to the public, the natural suspicions of the public would be sated. Just this past week we saw the example of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) reaching a private accommodation with Reader's Digest. I read a somewhat mysterious press release. The newspapers and political commentators spoke about it, and then we heard ministerial statements. The difference between what we are told by unofficial and by official sources makes us conscious of the existence of another hidden world. Many of us, even though we resist this tendency, become cynical. The evasions, the half truths and the falsities shine through the words and we are angered because we are treated somewhat like children. I submit to the treasury benches that only if politicians trust the public can they expect to deserve trust.
An editorial appeared in the Australian Federal Law Review and clearly stated the case when it said:
Unnecessary secrecy . . . has demonstrated an unfortunate pessimism as to the worth of the democratic process.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) makes statements, as he has been doing, calling into question the system and asking Canadians to join in the public debate about our institutions, I suggest-with much sincerity- that the very issue we are debating today is one of the reasons the public is profoundly cynical about the government. Ministerial responsibility is only possible in an open system where parliament-government and opposition- together with citizens gain knowledge of and access to greater information. "It is not that democracy functions better when there is open administration-until this exists, it is doubtful whether there is any democracy at all." So ends the editorial in the Australian Federal Law Review.
The truth is that if anything useful and significant is to be done in a free society, it must be done publicly and in such a way as to consult, involve and carry with it those affected. We are in an age where the legislator has assumed, I submit, a new role-that of building acceptance of government policy. It is not a role many people believe the opposition should have to carry, but in fact it is very

much a part of our role because a good deal of the legislation here, and a good many of the decisions of modern government, of course, have no ideological or partisan overtones. Therefore, we who believe in this institution are left with a responsibility to try to build public acceptance. But understanding and consent do not spring from some previous interaction of government and voter at a general election. Rather, it is the constantly renewed product of a continual exchange of information. In his book "Secrecy and Publicity", Francis Rourke observes:
-in so far as secrecy in government seriously impedes the free flow of communication among citizens, it constitutes a real threat to the informed public discussion that is at the core of democracy. Where this occurs, it is not at all certain that a community should not choose, from the point of view of its own value system, to tolerate some measure of insecurity in order to gain access to information it needs in order to exercise influence over decisions on vital matters of public policy.
I think that the public is mature enough-indeed, backbenchers opposite have shoulders broad enough-to deal with great issues such as the about-face of the Minister of National Revenue on Reader's Digest or a broader national debate prior to this government's agreement, for example, to sell nuclear reactors to South Korea and Argentina. I am not now debating whether that is right or wrong; I am debating the fact that we had information after the fact. Now, apparently, even the matter of interest is not to be disclosed. As the Globe and Mail's lead editorial of Tuesday, February 10, 1976 stated:
It is hard to conceive of a case when it should be more necessary that the government should act, not by executive, but by parliamentary decision. What is at stake is enormous ... It has almost reached the point of cliche to call this government arrogant. Unfortunately, it is a cliche full of truth.
A third example of where this government in recent weeks has demonstrated a gross lack of candour, openness and confidence in the ability of the public to examine the decision-making process in the bureaucracy is the stonewalling by the government of the efforts of the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments to gain information from the Department of Justice necessary for its deliberations. I feel genuinely concerned about the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), and the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) who spoke so eloquently just now-who have made the statutory instruments committee such an integral part of their contribution to the House over the past few years. Here we are, with the statutory instruments committee set up, the legislation in place, and we are being thwarted in our work by the Department of Justice because it takes a much too narrow and legalistic view of statutory instruments themselves. I really deplore this, and I deplore it doubly because the stonewalling comes from the Department of Justice of Canada.
In this regard I want to share with hon. members an eloquent statement made by the former minister of finance when he was minister of justice. In a speech at, I think, Harrison Hot Springs, when the Liberals were trying to give policy delineation for the years ahead, he said:
We have allowed, by enabling powers and statutes, legislation to be delegated to the cabinet, to ministers, to boards, to commissions by way of regulation ... beyond the control of parliament, beyond the power of parliament to review and revise, and thereby beyond the power of the people to challenge.
February 12, 1976

Now we have a committee which is attempting to make such regulations and administrative instruments accountable; in other words, to do what the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton wanted and give a major part of the government's policy initiatives to the Department of Justice. The government and its supporting bureaucracy continue to place roadblocks in the way of the efforts of this committee to do its job effectively. I think it is time these roadblocks were noticed by the public.
I, for one, deplore the fact that we have reached the unfortunate situation where governmental decisions affecting entire populations seem to be made by a few individuals operating on the basis of information with which they alone are familiar. Mr. Speaker, this is an intolerable situation. What can be done to combat this resistance to scrutiny, openness and candour? First, we should be told much more about the background against which decisions are made. Second, there is a vast, shaded area about which most of us know nothing and generally suspect the worst. Flitting in and out of the shadows are those "in the know" and those who wish to appear to be of that number. Goodness knows, in this city there are a lot of the latter. The nearer we are to the source of truth, the more we will hear-though not necessarily the more truths. Foreign affairs and defence are deepest in the shadow. We accept the necessity for some of this, but surely it is much overdone.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) reminded us that no rational member of parliament would ever think there should be disclosure of matters affecting the real, the genuine matter of national security. Nobody would expect such secrets to be open. But there is a huge, other area-up into the 90 per cent bracket-which has no possible bearing upon the security of the state. Third, when the government consults with private interests before finally taking decisions, could we not be told something of the bargains struck, the compromises reached, the promises given? I do not indict the compromises. Compromises are part of modern government. What I indict is the fact that nobody knows, except those intimately involved, what the options are.
Fourth-and not generally, I hope-the cabinet, its individual members and its supporting bureaucracy could afford to be much more open about policy objectives and national goals. Ministers seem to be genuinely fearful of being specific even about the ends they are seeking to achieve. Here is another caveat. If the Prime Minister hopes to enlist the public of this country in discussion- discussion with all of us in the new society-there have to be more slogans. The public is entitled to some declaration of the path the Prime Minister wishes to take us on behalf of his party.
I have to think that the reaction to the speech the Prime Minister made over Christmas was hilarious. If I have an objection to the speech, it is that it was so unclear-not that he made it. I think had such declarations been made in England, where there is a national press and a good differing of views and all the spectrum of political thought, they would have been scrutinized and recognized for what they were before the weekend was over. Instead of that, a good number of people in the Canadian Manufacturers' Association had cardiac arrests.

Statutory Instruments
Mr. Speaker, the problem we debate today is crucial to the creation of an environment in which our society can deal with the pressing economic and social issues which confront us daily. It seems apparent that we will have to deal increasingly with active government. In this milieu, the central question was put in a most interesting book written by Andrew Shonfield in 1965, wherein he asked:
The central question is how far an active government wielding great and varied economic power, intervening in the detailed conduct of private business affairs, discriminating between one citizen and another on the basis of subtle and complex judgments of the community's needs 10 or 20 years ahead, driving bargains with particular interest groups as administrative convenience dictates, can be subjected to effective democratic control.
That is the core of the debate in which we are engaged. I have not noticed very much partisanship here. This is surely the basis upon which the motion is put. It is surely the basis upon which the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments was brought to life by people who have honoured places in this House. On this issue we can agree that in eloquence nobody seeking this openness can match the hon. member for Peace River who has almost made a career of the subject.
